title: Record break; his own band and joining Papa Jack Laine's band
summary: After a record is played, he describes the Rockus band, other New Orleans bands, and leading Laine's band 1912-16.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Now, Nick, I think at this time we'll give them a fair sample of the kind of music that came from you when you were a very young man, so let them hear first. The Dixieland Jazz Band, which is actually the name of the song, it's the Dixieland Jazz Band, spelled J-A-S-S, which was the original spelling of jazz. Now, this recording was made many years ago and has been reissued, and the result is that it's not quite up to what we would like to call broadcast standard today, but it's still wonderful music. Let's hear it now. The Dixieland Jazz Band, ¶¶ ¶¶ ¶¶ And that was the original Dixieland jazz band playing a tune called the Dixieland Jazz Band. Now, we still have on the phone our old friend Nick LaRocka, the daddy, the granddaddy, the great-grandfather, calling what you want, of jazz. Now, Nick, let me talk to you. We had gotten up to about 1908, and by then you were just about to become a professional musician. Is that right?
Did you have a band of your own yet?
I did have a band. It was called the Rockus Band.
But I had played so much free music that people hired me and used to come get me for nothing, didn't want to pay me, so I started taking jobs with other bands.
Uh-huh. What other bands did you play with?
Well, I played with Joe Baraka, Leon Rapolo, and Bill Gallaty.
Susu Ramis, Harry Nunes, many bands. Then, around 1912, I was asked to play with Jack Lane.
Uh-huh. Oh, and this is the famous Papa Lane you used to call him.
That's right, old man Lane. He played ragtime drums, and he asked me if I'd take a job in his band.
And I'd take the job in his band, and I became the leader of that band up from around 1912 to 1916.
